To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the accumulation rate of carbon on a thin foil target irradiated with protons is proportional to the current density, independent of energy in the energy range of our investigation, and is strongly affected by the temperature of the foil target and the surrounding shield.
carbon is accumulated on the surface of a proton beam target at ¿ 2Å/min at ¿ 15° C and ¿ 0.2Å/min at 150° C.

the accumulation rate of carbon on a target surface irradiated by a proton beam increases with increasing current density, and is proportional at high current densities to the current density, is independent of proton energy in the range from 100 to 300 keV, increases with increasing target temperature in the range 0 to 150°C.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the accumulation of carbon on target surfaces irradiated by protons.
the interaction of energetic protons with carbon surfaces, and the effects of the surface conditions on the accumulation process.
the accumulation of carbon on surfaces irradiated by protons.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, at ¿ 100 keV, the accumulation of carbon on a thin metal target bombarded by protons is a function of the temperature of the metal and the temperature of the surrounding shield.
carbon is accumulated on target surfaces irradiated by protons, and that the accumulation rate depends on target temperature.
the observed beam spots on the front and the back surfaces of the thin target consist of accumulated carbon, and are proportional to the bombardement time at current densities ¿ 2¿ A/cm2.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the accumulation rate is proportional to the incident proton current density, is independent of energy for the range of our investigation, is reduced by cooling the target chamber, but not by heating the target.

the accumulation of carbon is a surface process, and is not due to the formation of a carbon film on the target surface, nor is the accumulation due to the implantation of carbon in the surface layers of the target.
, at ¿ 2Å/min accumulation rate, the beam spot is a carbon film, and that the accumulation is due to a chemical reaction between the beam and the target surface.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the accumulation rate is a function of the surface temperature.
the beam spot on the target is not a measure of the size of the proton beam.
the accumulation of carbon on the target surface is an important consideration in the design of proton accelerators.
